title: Μηναγύρται
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 236. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Μηναγύρται ὄνον ἔχοντες τούτῳ εἰώθεσαν τὰ σκεύη ἐπιτιθέντες ὁδοιπορεῖν.
sentences.tr: Mēnagyrtai onon echontes toutōi eiōthesan ta skeuē epitithentes hodoiporein.
sentences.l: Begging priests, having an ass, were accustomed to travel, placing their gear upon it.
sentences.i: Some begging priests had an ass, and it was their custom to load their gear on it and take the road.
sentences.n: μηναγύρται are itinerant alms-collectors who carried a god's holy things from town to town and lived on what they gathered; the name is built on Μήν, the moon-god, and the lexicon equates them with the μητραγύρται, the begging priests of the Mother. εἰώθεσαν is a pluperfect of εἴωθα, and since that perfect means simply 'am accustomed', the pluperfect means 'were accustomed'.

sentences.t: Καὶ δή ποτε ἀποθανόντος αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κόπου, ἐκδείραντες αὐτόν, ἐκ τοῦ δέρματος τύμπανα κατεσκεύασαν καὶ τούτοις ἔχρωντο.
sentences.tr: Kai dē pote apothanontos autou apo kopou, ekdeirantes auton, ek tou dermatos tympana kateskeuasan kai toutois echrōnto.
sentences.l: And indeed, it having died at some point of exhaustion, having flayed it, they made drums out of the hide and used those.
sentences.i: And when at last it died of exhaustion, they flayed it, made drums out of the hide, and used them.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute followed by a chain of aorist participles — the ordinary engine of these fables. τύμπανα are the hand-drums beaten in the ecstatic processions of these cults, so the ass becomes the instrument of the very trade that wore it to death.

sentences.t: Ἑτέρων δὲ αὐτοῖς μηναγυρτῶν ἀπαντησάντων καὶ πυνθανομένων αὐτῶν ποῦ εἴη ὁ ὄνος, ἔφασαν τεθνηκέναι μὲν αὐτόν, πληγὰς δὲ τοσαύτας λαμβάνειν ὅσας ποτὲ οὐδὲ ζῶν ὑπέμεινεν.
sentences.tr: Heterōn de autois mēnagyrtōn apantēsantōn kai pynthanomenōn autōn pou eiē ho onos, ephasan tethnēkenai men auton, plēgas de tosautas lambanein hosas pote oude zōn hypemeinen.
sentences.l: And other begging priests having met them and asking them where the ass was, they said that it had died, but was receiving as many blows as it never endured even while living.
sentences.i: When other begging priests met them and asked where the ass was, they said that it was dead, but was taking as many beatings as it had never endured while alive.
sentences.n: εἴη is the optative of the indirect question after a past main verb, the regular substitute for the indicative ἐστί of the direct question. τοσαύτας … ὅσας is the correlative pair, 'as many … as'. The μέν … δέ carries the joke: dead on one side of it, still being beaten on the other.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν οἰκετῶν ἔνιοι, καίπερ τῆς δουλείας ἀφειμένοι, τῶν δουλικῶν ἀρχῶν οὐκ ἀπαλλάττονται.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn oiketōn enioi, kaiper tēs douleias apheimenoi, tōn doulikōn archōn ouk apallattontai.
sentences.l: So too some of the household slaves, although released from slavery, are not rid of the servile offices.
sentences.i: So too some house-slaves, though set free from slavery, never get clear of a slave's duties.
sentences.n: καίπερ with a participle is the standing way of saying 'although'; ἀπαλλάττομαι and ἀφίημι both take the genitive of what one is freed from. τῶν δουλικῶν ἀρχῶν is the hard phrase: ἀρχή is either a beginning or an office of authority, and neither sits perfectly here. 'The offices that belong to slaves' — the tasks and the subjection that go with them — fits the dead ass who is still beaten; a sense 'their servile origins' is possible but weaker.
